slides.title: A savings plan with a calculation you can inspect
slides.subtitle: GoalWise takes a user from one target date to a weekly plan, then shows how the number was produced.
bullets: One goal. Explicit assumptions. A result the user can review.
Live demo: registration -> setup -> plan -> explanation.
slides.notes: Presenter: Vishal. 0:45. Start with the product question, not the technology. GoalWise is a focused planning workflow: one savings goal, explicit assumptions, and a weekly result that the team can trace back to its inputs.

slides.title: We started with one planning question
slides.subtitle: Can this user reach the target by the target date, and what can they spend this week?
bullets: One active savings goal
Manual income and planned expense inputs
Backend-owned dashboard values
Structured planning CSV import with preview and confirmation
CSV preview + confirmation and an optional AI explanation
Outside this demo: bank sync, raw transactions, and multiple active goals
slides.notes: Presenter: Vishal. 0:55. Define the boundary before discussing implementation. The current product is the planning loop, not a general personal-finance system. CSV import and the AI explanation are controlled edges around that loop; bank sync, raw transaction import, and multiple active goals are outside this demo.

slides.title: The browser collects inputs; the backend decides what they mean
slides.subtitle: The UI guides the user, while validation, ownership, calculation, and persistence stay server-side.
bullets: React + Vite frontend over versioned /api/v1 JSON
FastAPI service layer owns validation and ownership checks
Pure pace engine returns deterministic pace-v1 results
SQLAlchemy/Alembic persist PostgreSQL-compatible records
Snapshots and dashboard read model expose committed results
slides.notes: Presenter: Nati. 1:00. Walk through the request path: the React UI sends inputs to the versioned FastAPI API; services validate and normalize them; the pure pace engine calculates the result; the database stores the committed snapshot; the dashboard reads the backend response. React formats the number but does not reproduce the formula.

slides.title: The weekly allowance is calculated in one place
slides.subtitle: The backend produces safe-to-spend, shortfall, and pace status from versioned inputs.
bullets: Decision: keep official financial output in pace-v1.
Evidence: identical inputs produce the same result; golden tests cover the calculation contract.
Alternative rejected: an AI-generated number would be harder to reproduce and audit.
Trade-off: the formula is narrower than open-ended financial advice.
Consequence: explanations can add context without changing the number.
slides.notes: Presenter: Nati. 1:00. This is the main technical decision. The number has to be reproducible because it is the product's most consequential output. We accepted a narrower formula in exchange for a result we can test, explain, and defend.

slides.title: A saved plan should explain its own history
slides.subtitle: Each committed calculation records normalized inputs, outputs, and the formula version that produced them.
bullets: Decision: write a new immutable snapshot after a committed plan change.
Evidence: the snapshot schema stores normalized aggregates and formula_version.
Alternative rejected: recomputing history would erase what the user saw earlier.
Trade-off: more records and more schema discipline.
Boundary: raw transaction descriptions do not enter the durable result.
slides.notes: Presenter: Nati. 0:55. A snapshot gives the dashboard and the explanation a stable reference. When the plan changes, the system creates a new record instead of silently rewriting the old result. That makes the calculation reviewable during the demo and later.

slides.title: The deployed app does not trust the browser with ownership
slides.subtitle: Sessions, CSRF checks, and server-side ownership rules protect the same workflow we demo locally.
bullets: HTTP-only server-side sessions with hashed opaque tokens
CSRF required for authenticated unsafe methods
Cross-user private resource access returns 404
Railway uses secure cookies, explicit origin allowlists, and PostgreSQL
Failure case: unauthorized or cross-user access fails without leaking private data
slides.notes: Presenter: Nati. 0:55. Security is part of the product contract, not a deployment footnote. The browser can request a resource, but the backend decides whether the session owns it. We will use invalid CSV as the visible demo failure; the cross-user access tests are the stronger evidence behind the same trust boundary.

slides.title: The summary is downstream of the calculation
slides.subtitle: The model receives a minimized snapshot and writes explanation text; the official numbers remain unchanged.
bullets: Runtime AI receives minimized aggregate fields from an existing snapshot
Generated explanations are schema-checked and tied to the displayed snapshot
AI cannot calculate, override, or recommend official money outputs
Development AI use is reviewed against repo evidence before claims enter the deck
slides.notes: Presenter: Nati. 0:55. The team used AI heavily during implementation, but the specification, boundaries, and review process remained human-guided. At runtime, the model only sees minimized aggregate data from an existing snapshot. It can explain that result, but it cannot calculate, override, or turn it into financial advice.

slides.title: We tested the contracts that support the demo
slides.subtitle: The project is deployed through GitHub CI/CD to Railway, with evidence at the calculation, API, UI, and delivery boundaries.
bullets: Calculation: pace-v1 golden scenarios
API: auth, ownership, financial inputs, CSV import, and AI routes
Persistence: migration smoke checks for PostgreSQL-compatible storage
UI and delivery: TypeScript, lint, Vite, Playwright, GitHub CI, and Railway
Known limit: these checks do not prove production-scale load behavior
slides.notes: Presenter: Thanh. 1:00. Tie each evidence group to a system boundary: pace-v1 golden tests for the financial contract; API and cross-user tests for behavior and ownership; migration checks for persistence; frontend checks for the build and user flow; GitHub CI and Railway deployment for delivery. These checks support the demo, but they do not prove production-scale load behavior.

slides.title: We will follow one user through the system
slides.subtitle: Registration, setup, plan creation, a rejected import, seeded data, and a snapshot-backed explanation.
bullets: Value path: register, follow the starter guide, create a goal, and read the dashboard
Failure path: submit an invalid CSV and show that it is rejected before commit
Evidence path: load seeded data, generate the summary, then show CI/CD and Railway
Transition: browser first; repository and deployment evidence second
slides.notes: Presenter: Vishal, then demo operator. 0:25. Hand off directly to the browser. Start at https://goalwise.up.railway.app/register. Use https://staging-goalwise.up.railway.app/register as the fallback. The visible failure is an invalid CSV import: the app should reject it during review rather than changing the plan. Then use seeded data to show the dashboard and generate the AI summary.
